subject: Mathematics
title: Raj and Priya's Village Map Adventure
hook: Help Raj and Priya find their way around the village using maps and directions.

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: Raj's clever cousin with a compass

slides.title: Maps and Locations
slides.storyContext: Raj and Priya arrive at their grandmother's village for summer holidays. Dadi pulls out an old hand-drawn map of the village and asks them to help find the local temple for evening prayers.
slides.inSimpleWords: A map is a picture that shows where things are in a place.

slides.title: The Mystery of Dadi's Map
slides.storyContext: Dadi shows them her hand-drawn village map with the school, temple, marketplace, well, and her house marked. Raj gets excited: 'But Dadi, how do we know which way is north?' Priya pulls out a small compass from her pocket. Together, they realize the map has a compass rose drawn in the corner showing North, South, East, and West.
slides.inSimpleWords: Maps use directions like North, South, East, and West to show us how to get places.

slides.title: Directions: The Four Cardinal Points
slides.storyContext: Standing in the middle of the village square, Dadi points: 'North is where the mountains are, South toward the river, East toward the sunrise, West toward the sunset.' Raj repeats the directions: North-East-South-West, and Priya adds, 'And we can remember it as NEWS!'

points.label: Cardinal Directions
points.text: North (N) = up, South (S) = down, East (E) = right (sunrise), West (W) = left (sunset)

points.label: Compass Rose
points.text: A symbol on the map showing these four directions

points.label: Finding your way
points.text: Always look for the compass rose to know which way to go

example.problem: If you are at Dadi's house facing the temple which is to the North, where would you turn to face the marketplace which is to the East?
example.solution: You would turn 90° to your right (clockwise) to face East.

slides.inSimpleWords: Directions help us know which way to go: North is up, South is down, East is right, West is left.

image.prompt: a compass rose with N, S, E, W marked, surrounded by a village with a temple to the north and a marketplace to the east

slides.title: Grid Lines: Making a Square Map
slides.storyContext: Priya draws a grid on Dadi's map using a ruler. 'Now we can find any place using rows and columns, like a checkerboard!' Each square in the grid is labeled. Dadi's house is in the square at Column B, Row 2. Raj picks a red crayon and marks it.

points.label: Grid
points.text: A pattern of lines that form squares on a map

points.label: Rows
points.text: Horizontal lines numbered from bottom (1) to top (for vertical position)

points.label: Columns
points.text: Vertical lines labeled A, B, C, D... from left to right (for horizontal position)

points.label: Grid Reference
points.text: Combining column letter and row number tells you exactly where something is

example.problem: The well is at column D, row 3. The school is at column B, row 4. Describe their positions on the grid.
example.solution: Well is in column D (4th column from left), row 3 (3rd row from bottom). School is in column B (2nd column from left), row 4 (4th row from bottom).

slides.inSimpleWords: A grid is like a checkerboard on the map. We use letters for columns and numbers for rows to pinpoint any location.

image.prompt: a village map with a grid overlay, columns labeled A through E and rows numbered 1 through 5, with houses, a temple, and a well marked at specific grid positions

slides.title: Scale: Measuring Real Distances
slides.storyContext: Raj asks: 'Dadi, if the temple is just 1 cm away on your map, how far is it to really walk there?' Dadi smiles and points to the corner of her map: 'See this line marked 1 cm = 100 meters? That's the scale. So 1 cm on my map is 100 meters in real life.'

points.label: Map Scale
points.text: A ratio showing how map distance relates to real-world distance

points.label: Example scales
points.text: 1 cm = 100 m (small village), 1 cm = 1 km (larger area), 1 inch = 1 mile (very large areas)

points.label: Using scale
points.text: Measure the distance on the map, then multiply by the scale to find the real distance

example.problem: On Dadi's map, the distance from school to the marketplace is 3 cm. If the scale is 1 cm = 100 m, how far is it really?
example.solution: 3 cm × 100 m per cm = 300 meters in real life.

slides.inSimpleWords: Scale tells us how big real things actually are compared to the map. A small line on the map might mean a long walk in real life.

image.prompt: a ruler next to a map of a village, showing '1 cm = 100 meters' scale, with children measuring the distance from school to market

slides.title: Symbols on Maps: A Secret Code
slides.storyContext: Priya flips to the back of Dadi's map and finds a legend: a small temple symbol ⛩️, a school symbol 🏫, a house symbol 🏠, and a tree symbol 🌳. 'Dadi, this is like a secret code! Each symbol means something different,' she exclaims. Dadi nods: 'Yes, without the legend, we wouldn't know what we're looking at.'

points.label: Map Legend
points.text: A key that explains what each symbol or color on the map means

points.label: Common symbols
points.text: Houses (small squares), schools (flag), temples (spire), trees (green dots), rivers (blue wavy lines)

points.label: Why symbols?
points.text: Drawing real pictures would make the map too crowded; symbols are simple and clear

example.problem: On a map legend, you see: ⛩️ = temple, 🏥 = health center, 💧 = well. If there are 3 wells marked on the map, how many sources of water does the village have?
example.solution: At least 3, though there may be more wells not marked on the map.

slides.inSimpleWords: Map symbols are like a picture code. A legend tells you what each symbol means.

image.prompt: a map legend showing colorful symbols: temple, school, house, well, tree, and river with labels next to each

slides.title: Different Types of Maps
slides.storyContext: At Dadi's house, Raj finds three different maps in a drawer: a hand-drawn village map (physical features like rivers and trees), a road map with marked routes, and a thematic map showing where crops grow. 'Which one is best?' he asks. Priya says, 'They show different things! We choose based on what we need to find.'

points.label: Physical Maps
points.text: Show natural features: rivers, mountains, forests, valleys

points.label: Political Maps
points.text: Show borders, states, cities, countries

points.label: Road/Street Maps
points.text: Show streets, highways, landmarks for navigation

points.label: Thematic Maps
points.text: Show specific information like weather, population, or crop distribution

slides.inSimpleWords: Different maps show different information. Pick the right map for what you want to find out.

image.prompt: three maps side by side: a physical map with rivers and mountains, a political map with boundaries, and a crop distribution map with colored regions

slides.title: Reading Dadi's Village Map: A Full Task
slides.storyContext: Now Raj and Priya are ready for the real challenge. Dadi hands them the village map and asks them to plan a route from her house to the marketplace, passing by the school. They use the grid references, cardinal directions, and the scale to plan their walk.

example.problem: Using the village map (scale: 1 cm = 100 m, grid shown), Dadi's house is at B2, the school is at C3, and the marketplace is at D2. Plan a route and calculate the total walking distance. Which direction from school leads to the marketplace?
example.solution: Route: Start at B2 (Dadi's house) → go East and North to C3 (school) → then go East and South to D2 (marketplace). Direction from school to market: East and South (Southeast). Distance: approximately 2.5 cm on map = 250 meters in real life.

slides.inSimpleWords: Reading a map means using the grid, directions, and scale together to find places and measure distances.

slides.title: Can You Find the Hidden Well?
slides.storyContext: Dadi gives Raj and Priya a challenge before dinner: 'There's a well hidden on the eastern edge of the village. It's 2 cm from the marketplace according to the scale. Can you find it on the map?' Raj and Priya work together, measuring, looking at the scale, and checking the compass rose.

example.problem: Starting from the marketplace at D2, go 2 cm due East (right) on a map with scale 1 cm = 100 m. What is the real distance, and approximately at which grid position should the well be?
example.solution: Real distance: 2 cm × 100 m/cm = 200 meters. The well would be approximately at E2 on the grid (one column to the right, same row).

slides.inSimpleWords: Using a map, you can find hidden places by following directions and using the scale.

slides.title: What We Learned Today
slides.storyContext: As the sun sets, Raj and Priya sit with Dadi, proudly holding the map. 'We found everything we needed,' says Priya. Dadi smiles: 'You learned to read a map like true explorers.'

points.label: Directions
points.text: North, South, East, West (NEWS) help us know which way to go

points.label: Grid
points.text: Columns (letters) and rows (numbers) pinpoint exact locations

points.label: Scale
points.text: Tells us how map distance relates to real distance

points.label: Symbols & Legend
points.text: A key code that explains what each symbol means

points.label: Map Types
points.text: Different maps show different information; choose the right one for your need

slides.inSimpleWords: Maps are tools that help us find our way. With directions, a grid, scale, and symbols, we can navigate anywhere.

subject: Mathematics
title: Amir's Mango Market Data Adventure
hook: Learn to read and create pictographs and bar graphs using a real village fruit market.

characters.name: Amir
characters.role: the fruit vendor's son learning to count sales

characters.name: Neha
characters.role: Amir's friend who loves puzzles and patterns

characters.name: Mr. Verma
characters.role: the market vendor who teaches data collection

slides.title: Data Through Pictures
slides.storyContext: Amir's father owns a fruit stall in the village market. Every day, he sells mangoes, bananas, oranges, and apples. But he never remembers which fruit sells best! Neha suggests: 'Let's collect data and show it with pictures. Then you'll know at a glance!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Data is information we collect. Pictures help us understand data quickly.

slides.title: Collecting Fruit Sales Data
slides.storyContext: For one week, Amir and Neha keep a tally. Every time someone buys mangoes, they draw one dot. Bananas get a mark, oranges get a mark, apples get a mark. By Sunday, they have hundreds of marks! Mr. Verma, the elderly shop owner next door, watches them and says, 'You're doing what shops call data collection. Now organize it so we can see the real story.'
slides.inSimpleWords: We collect data by counting or recording things. A tally mark or tally table helps us keep track.

slides.title: Tally Marks: Counting Made Easy
slides.storyContext: Neha shows Amir the tally method. 'Every line is one item. But at five, we cross the diagonal line through four others, making a group of five. Then we count faster!' They organize their fruit sales: Mangoes ⊢⊣⊢ (13), Bananas ⊢⊣⊢⊣ (19), Oranges ⊢⊣ (8), Apples ⊢⊣⊢⊣⊢⊣ (25).

points.label: Tally Mark
points.text: A single line (|) representing one count

points.label: Grouped Tally
points.text: Four vertical lines crossed by a diagonal line (⊢⊣) represents 5 items

points.label: Counting Tallies
points.text: Count groups of 5, then add remaining individual marks

points.label: Why tallies?
points.text: Easier than writing numbers, and grouped marks help us count faster

example.problem: Amir makes these tallies for Saturday sales: Mangoes ⊢⊣⊢| (11 marks). How many mangoes were sold?

slides.inSimpleWords: Tally marks help us count quickly. Groups of 5 (crossed line) make counting easier.

image.prompt: tally marks showing groups of 5 crossed marks and individual marks, representing fruit sales: mangoes, bananas, oranges, apples

slides.title: Pictographs: Using Pictures to Show Data
slides.storyContext: Neha says, 'What if instead of numbers, we draw little pictures?' She draws a small mango symbol 🥭 for each item sold. But since 25 apples is too many drawings, Mr. Verma suggests: 'One big apple picture can mean 5 apples sold. That way, we use fewer pictures but still show the same data!'

points.label: Pictograph
points.text: A graph using small pictures or symbols instead of numbers

points.label: Picture Symbol
points.text: Represents one or more items (e.g., one 🥭 = 1 mango, or one 🍎 = 5 apples)

points.label: Key/Scale
points.text: Shows what each picture means (e.g., '1 picture = 5 items')

points.label: Partial pictures
points.text: Half a picture means half the value (e.g., half of 5 apples = 2.5 apples)

example.problem: A pictograph shows oranges sold using 🍊 symbols. The key says 1 🍊 = 3 oranges. If there are 3 full symbols and 1 half symbol, how many oranges were sold?

slides.inSimpleWords: A pictograph uses pictures to show data. Each picture can mean 1 item or many items, based on the key.

image.prompt: a simple pictograph with mango symbols representing weekly sales: mangoes (13), bananas (19), oranges (8), apples (25), with a key showing '1 mango symbol = 5 mangoes sold'

slides.title: Bar Graphs: Data in Columns
slides.storyContext: Mr. Verma pulls out a chart drawn on grid paper. 'This is a bar graph. Each fruit gets a column, and the height of the column shows how many sold.' Amir sees vertical bars for each fruit. Bananas have the tallest bar (19), so they sold best. Oranges have the shortest bar (8). 'So bananas are our winner!' exclaims Neha.

points.label: Bar Graph
points.text: Uses vertical (or horizontal) bars to compare quantities

points.label: Axis Labels
points.text: X-axis (horizontal) shows categories (mangoes, bananas, etc.), Y-axis (vertical) shows the count

points.label: Bar Height/Length
points.text: Represents the value for each category; taller/longer bar = larger quantity

points.label: Reading Bars
points.text: Look at where the top of each bar aligns with the scale on the Y-axis

example.problem: A bar graph shows fruit sales: Mangoes bar reaches 13, Bananas bar reaches 19, Oranges bar reaches 8, Apples bar reaches 25. Which fruit was the most sold? Which was the least sold?
example.solution: Most sold: Apples (25). Least sold: Oranges (8).

slides.inSimpleWords: A bar graph uses tall or short bars to compare numbers. Taller bar = bigger number.

image.prompt: a bar graph with vertical bars for mangoes, bananas, oranges, and apples, each bar reaching different heights on a grid, with Y-axis labeled 0-30 and X-axis labeled with fruit names

slides.title: Creating Your Own Bar Graph
slides.storyContext: Amir decides to make his own bar graph on grid paper. He writes the fruit names along the bottom (X-axis) and numbers (0–30) along the side (Y-axis). For each fruit, he colors in squares from the bottom up to the number sold. Neha checks his work: 'Perfect! Now anyone can see that bananas and apples are our bestsellers.'

points.label: Step 1: Draw Axes
points.text: Draw a horizontal line (X-axis) and vertical line (Y-axis)

points.label: Step 2: Label Axes
points.text: X-axis gets categories (fruit names); Y-axis gets numbers (count scale)

points.label: Step 3: Draw Bars
points.text: For each category, draw a bar reaching up to the correct number

points.label: Step 4: Color/Shade
points.text: Fill or color the bars so they stand out; add a title

example.problem: You have data: Apples 12, Bananas 18, Grapes 10, Oranges 15. Create a bar graph with X-axis labeled with fruit names and Y-axis numbered 0–20.
example.solution: Draw four bars: Apples bar to 12, Bananas bar to 18, Grapes bar to 10, Oranges bar to 15. Ensure each bar's top aligns with its number on the Y-axis.

slides.inSimpleWords: Making a bar graph: draw two lines (axes), label them, then draw bars for each category up to its number.

image.prompt: a person drawing a bar graph on grid paper, using a ruler and colored pencils, with labeled X and Y axes, and bars of varying heights for different fruit types

slides.title: Comparing and Interpreting Graphs
slides.storyContext: Amir's father looks at the bar graph and says, 'So we sold 25 apples and 19 bananas, but only 8 oranges. That means people prefer apples and bananas. Maybe I should buy more apple trees!' Neha adds, 'And we know exactly how much more: 25 − 8 = 17 more apples than oranges.'

points.label: Comparison
points.text: Bar graphs let us compare quantities at a glance (which is biggest, smallest, equal)

points.label: Finding Differences
points.text: Subtract one value from another (e.g., 25 − 8 = 17 more apples than oranges)

points.label: Finding Totals
points.text: Add all bars together to find total sales (e.g., 13 + 19 + 8 + 25 = 65 total fruits)

points.label: Making Decisions
points.text: Data guides real-world choices (stock more of bestsellers, less of slow items)

example.problem: Bar graph shows: Monday 12 customers, Tuesday 18 customers, Wednesday 10 customers, Thursday 15 customers. How many more customers came on Tuesday than Wednesday? What was the total for the week so far?
example.solution: Tuesday − Wednesday = 18 − 10 = 8 more customers on Tuesday. Total = 12 + 18 + 10 + 15 = 55 customers.

slides.inSimpleWords: Graphs help us compare and make real decisions. We can see which is biggest, find differences, and add totals.

image.prompt: a bar graph with annotations pointing to bars: 'tallest bar = most popular', 'this bar is 7 more than that bar', 'add all bars for total'

slides.title: A Week of Market Data: The Full Story
slides.storyContext: Amir and Neha collect data for an entire week and present it to Mr. Verma. They create both a pictograph and a bar graph. Mr. Verma studies them carefully and says, 'Excellent work! Now I see the real story of my market. Let's use this to plan next month.'

example.problem: Weekly fruit sales: Mon (M=5, B=7, O=3, A=8), Tue (M=6, B=9, O=4, A=10), Wed (M=4, B=5, O=2, A=6), Thu (M=7, B=10, O=5, A=12), Fri (M=8, B=12, O=6, A=14). Create a pictograph using symbols where 1 symbol = 2 fruits. Also, calculate total apples sold for the week.
example.solution: Monday total: 5+7+3+8 = 23 fruits. Tuesday total: 6+9+4+10 = 29 fruits. Wednesday total: 4+5+2+6 = 17 fruits. Thursday total: 7+10+5+12 = 34 fruits. Friday total: 8+12+6+14 = 40 fruits. Total apples for week: 8+10+6+12+14 = 50 apples. Pictograph: Each day gets symbols for each fruit type, with each symbol representing 2 fruits.

slides.inSimpleWords: Real data from a week tells a big story. Both pictographs and bar graphs help us see patterns and trends.

slides.title: Mystery: Which Fruit Wins?
slides.storyContext: Neha challenges Amir: 'I've made a bar graph of sales for the last 10 days, but I mixed up the labels! Bananas, Oranges, Apples, and Mangoes are jumbled. The bar heights are 10, 18, 12, and 25. Can you figure out which fruit is which based on what we know sells best?'

example.problem: Four bars show: 10, 18, 12, and 25. Based on the previous week's data (Apples were highest, Oranges were lowest), assign fruit names to each bar.
example.solution: Most likely: Apples = 25 (highest), Bananas = 18, Mangoes = 12, Oranges = 10 (lowest). This matches the pattern from last week where apples were popular and oranges sold the least.

slides.inSimpleWords: Sometimes we need to use patterns and logic to read graphs, not just the numbers.

slides.title: The Market Data Story
slides.storyContext: At the end of the week, Amir's father thanks both children. 'You've taught me to see my business through data. I now know exactly which fruits to stock and which to reduce. That's the power of data!' Neha smiles: 'And it all started with simple pictures and bars.'

points.label: Tally Marks
points.text: Help us count data quickly using groups of 5

points.label: Pictographs
points.text: Use pictures and symbols to show data; each picture has a fixed value

points.label: Bar Graphs
points.text: Use vertical or horizontal bars to compare quantities

points.label: Interpreting Data
points.text: We can compare (bigger, smaller), find differences, and make real decisions based on graphs

points.label: Data in Real Life
points.text: Markets, schools, hospitals use graphs to make smart choices

slides.inSimpleWords: Graphs turn numbers into pictures. Pictures make it easy to understand data and make good decisions.
